A safe MCP/PHP implementation should advertise and enforce a restricted local JSON Schema 2020-12 profile, not imply universal 2020-12 support. MCP tools use inputSchema for arguments and may expose outputSchema; servers must return conforming structured results, while clients should validate them.

## Two distinct validations

- Schema admission (meta-validation): parse the schema as JSON, select the allowed dialect/profile, and validate its syntax against a local meta-schema/policy. A meta-schema describes schemas and their permitted vocabulary/syntax; it does not prove that any tool arguments satisfy the schema.
- Instance validation: validate the actual decoded tool arguments or produced structuredContent against an already-admitted, compiled schema. JSON Schema assertions yield a boolean result for an instance.
Reject schemas outside the profile at registration/load time: unsupported keywords/vocabularies, $dynamicRef/$dynamicAnchor, unsupported regex features, or unresolved references. This is intentionally stricter than JSON Schema’s interoperability fallback, under which unknown individual keywords can be treated as annotations.

## Preserve JSON semantics in PHP

Decode a JSON request once into a JSON-compatible tree:
- JSON object → associative PHP array/map.
- JSON array → sequential PHP array/list, retaining whether it was an object or array.
- JSON integer token → PHP int only when representable; otherwise preserve an exact numeric representation or reject it under an explicit profile limit.
- JSON fractional/exponent number → do not silently coerce to int; preserve decimal semantics (for example, string-backed decimal) or define/reject the supported numeric range.
This matters because JSON Schema’s data model distinguishes object, array, number, and string; it does not distinguish integer from other numbers at the core-data-model level, though the validation vocabulary supplies integer. It also warns that language parsers may not represent every JSON value in memory.

## Composition and formats

allOf and $ref apply multiple subschemas; therefore “no extra fields” must be evaluated only after considering the effective composed schema. Do not implement additionalProperties: false as a shallow, local properties check that rejects fields supplied by a referenced or allOf branch. Applicators combine subschema results, including referenced schemas.
Treat format as annotation unless the profile explicitly enables the Format-Assertion vocabulary and has full validators for every declared format. Draft 2020-12 separates format-annotation from optional format-assertion; an implementation claiming the latter but lacking full format validation must refuse the schema.

## References and resource bounds

Preload a finite reference closure: every accepted $ref resolves only to a registered local schema resource or same-document pointer/anchor. Resolve and compile it before invocation; never fetch URLs during validation. That eliminates validation-triggered network access and SSRF. OWASP recommends positive allowlists rather than deny-lists for outbound destinations; the strongest profile needs no outbound reference fetching at all.
Set hard limits before evaluation: schema bytes, reference count/depth, $ref cycle policy, nesting depth, instance bytes/depth, object members/array items, regex length and match time, evaluation steps, wall-clock timeout, and error count. Reject or return a validation-resource-exhausted error—never continue with a partially evaluated schema.

## Output after effects

Validate output before publishing it, but an invalid output after the tool performed a side effect does not mean the effect was rolled back. The action may already have created a record, charged an account, sent a message, or committed remotely; output validation only says the returned representation violates the contract.
Do not automatically retry merely because output validation failed: the retry can duplicate the effect. Return an explicit “execution outcome uncertain / output-contract failure,” persist an operation ID and audit record, and reconcile by querying the authoritative system. Automatic retry is appropriate only when the operation has a verified idempotency key or a documented read-only/transactionally reversible boundary. MCP itself separates protocol/tool execution errors and advises validating results, but schema failure is not a transaction protocol.
